processing: Mostly deep-steamed as fukamushi sencha, often with a week of shade before picking, which tames its natural astringency and improves the colour.
harvest_season: Very early spring, about 5 days before Yabukita; early first-flush lots are the ones marketed as new tea.
appearance_dry: Typical of fukamushi: small, dark green, somewhat broken needles.
appearance_liquor: Dark, cloudy green, as with deep-steamed sencha.
appearance_wet: Soft, fine, dark green leaf pieces, as with other fukamushi.
taste_profile: Mild and rounded when deep-steamed, with astringency and sweetness in balance.

brewing.notes: Fine fukamushi leaf steeps fast, so keep the first steep short and use a fine-mesh strainer.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's harvest, and it comes early because Kagoshima leads the Japanese season. It is widely used in blends as well as sold under its own name. Drink it within about a year.
description:
Yutakamidori is the cultivar behind much of Kagoshima's green tea. It suits warm southern Japan and is one of the prevalent cultivars in the prefecture's tea fields. One cultivar reference ranks it second only to Yabukita by planted area in Japan.

It buds early, about five days before Yabukita, and yields better. It is strong against anthracnose but sensitive to cold and frost, which is why it stays in the south.

Processed as regular sencha it can be quite astringent with a poor colour. Deep steaming and a week of shade solved this, and now it is known for a dark green liquor with a mild, sweet balance. Keep steeps short, since the fine leaf gives up flavour quickly.

Look for Kagoshima on the label and a current harvest year. Try it beside a Saemidori, Kagoshima's other big cultivar, to feel the difference.
history:
Yutakamidori grew from Asatsuyu seed at the Ministry of Agriculture's tea site in Kanaya, Shizuoka. The best seedling was selected in 1949 as Y-2, and the name was registered in Kagoshima Prefecture in 1966. It is described as not nationally registered.

It found its home in Kagoshima, and processing changes there turned an astringent plant into a marketable fukamushi tea.
